newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH- Treasury reveals budget's economic impact.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH- Treasury reveals budget's economic impact.

text.p: One of the great themes of Australian economics this year has been the debate over budget cuts and their direct economic impact -- the old Keynesian theory once well accepted but now disputed by officialdom.
So how much GDP do we lose when the government withdraws fiscal stimulus worth A$7.2 billion in 1997/98?
The answer, from Treasury Deputy Secretary Gary Potts: 0.25 percent, and it's factored into the 1997/98 GDP projection.
Potts was one of several Treasury officials, including Secretary Ted Evans, who was quizzed about the department's estimates before a Senate committee on Monday evening.
As usual, Senators used the "domestic economy" expenditure line item as an excuse to wander backwards and forwards across Treasury's forecasts.
Opposition finance spokesman Nick Sherry was most interested in backing up Labor's line that the budget cuts are bad for activity.
Undeniably, there must be some minor negative impact in the short term, but the government has avoided the question like the plague.
So Potts' first answer to the question was: "In the budget forecasts themselves, the forecasts incorporate a small reduction in the growth outlook as a result of the fiscal consolidation."

But later Sherry asked him about the GDP "projections" -- the unreliable distant economic outlook which is needed for the fiscal forward estimates but which Treasury does not want to take much responsibility for.
These figures show 3.25 percent GDP growth in 1997/98, and 3.5 percent in 1998/99 and 1999/00.
Potts explained that 3.5 percent was considered a reasonable expectation of long-run growth (he would have said "as good a guess as any", but that wouldn't be Treasury-like).
So why only 3.25 percent in 1997/98?
"Well, we thought it was appropriate to allow for the effects of fiscal consolidation but to go no further than that in attempting to produce forecasts which would allow for cyclical effets."
That is, 1997/98 would have had 3.5 percent pencilled in as a cyclically average number, but Treasury felt it had to make some allowance for the budget.
"So we were simply allowing for the impact of the fiscal consolidation in very broad terms," Potts said.
Note that the bulk of budget measures will not operate until next calendar year.
With a bit of a lag, that would put the effect on demand into 1997/98, as Treasury estimates.
The political implication of all this is interesting.
Sherry must have been hoping that Potts would divulge a 0.5 percent loss of GDP from the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus.
That would have translated into about 40,000 jobs (0.5 percent of the 8 million strong workforce).
Still, 0.25 percent is 20,000 jobs, but economics is no precise science and the Opposition would need evidence of really big job sacrifices to make much of a running on the issue.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
